title: Improved denoising diffusion probabilistic models with efficient non-diagonal covariance modeling

paper.title: Improved denoising diffusion probabilistic models with efficient non-diagonal covariance modeling
paper.abstract:
Abstract The sampling process of Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) can be accelerated by leveraging second-order information in the form of approximations to the denoising posterior covariance – allowing samples of acceptable quality to be produced in fewer but larger sampling steps.
Previous attempts at using such information have used drastic (e.g. diagonal) simplifications of the covariance.
These do not do justice to the peculiar statistical structure of natural images, which exhibit strong non-diagonal correlations between pixels and color channels, and a slow-decaying power-law frequency spectrum.
Here, we develop a novel covariance model that captures these features. Our Kronecker-DCT (K-DCT) model uses a Kronecker-factored decomposition of inter-color covariances and spatial covariances modeled in the frequency domain using the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT).
The use of the DCT reduces the computational complexity from quadratic to log-linear, resulting in negligible computational and memory overhead in each denoising step.
By learning K-DCT-structured amortizations of the denoising posterior covariance using pre-trained score models on CIFAR-10, Celeb-A, ImageNet and LSUN datasets, we show improved performance compared to previous SOTA denoising samplers, both in terms of FID and likelihoods, especially in the regime of few denoising steps.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs; 15 ; 38 ; 40 ) are a family of generative models used ubiquitously for image generation ( 33 ; 10 ; 4 ) , where they give state-of-the-art performance both in terms of fidelity (quality of samples) and mode-coverage (sample diversity). These models sample new images by running a so-called ‘denoising’ Markov chain, starting from pure noise. Given the current image 𝒙 t \bm{x}_{t} at time step t t , a slightly less noisy image 𝒙 t − δ \bm{x}_{t-\delta} is obtained by sampling from a Gaussian approximation to the ‘denoising posterior’ p ⁡ ( 𝒙 t − δ | 𝒙 t ) p(\bm{x}_{t-\delta}|\bm{x}_{t}) , under a certain probabilistic model that defines their joint distribution. Most research efforts so far have focused on approximating the first moment of this posterior, i.e. the conditional mean 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝒙 t − δ | 𝒙 t ] \mathbb{E}[\bm{x}_{t-\delta}|\bm{x}_{t}] , using deep networks trained through various objectives. The main justification for not paying much attention to the second-order moment (i.e. Cov ​ [ 𝒙 t − δ | 𝒙 t ] \text{Cov}[\bm{x}_{t-\delta}|\bm{x}_{t}] ) is that, with enough, and small enough, denoising steps, the posterior covariance has a simple (diagonal) form available in closed-form ( 1 ; 38 ) . However, taking many small steps in an inherently sequential algorithm is not easily parallelized, such that a trade-off arises between sample quality and sampling time. To speed up image generation, one can formulate diffusion in the (smaller) latent space of a pretrained image autoencoder ( 33 ) , express the stochastic denoising process as an equivalent deterministic ODE that can be accelerated by appropriate choices of (e.g. higher-order) ODE solvers ( 38 ; 21 ; 18 ; 44 ; 46 ; 6 ) , or outright distill the sampling process into a one-step network ( 22 ; 45 ) . Although distilled one-step samplers dominate current practice by offering fast, high-quality generation, they lose the benefit of DDPM’s tractable likelihood estimation. Here, we follow another line of recent research that has shown that standard DDPM sampling can be accelerated by performing fewer but larger steps. This increased efficiency is achieved by using a more accurate model of the posterior covariance ( 3 ; 2 ; 28 ; 31 ) . As it turns out, any score network that has been (well) trained to approximate the posterior mean contains all the information needed to estimate the covariance, too. This relationship has been formalized recently through a generalization of Tweedie’s formula ( 9 ) to higher order moments ( 23 ) , revealing an analytical relation between high-order posterior moments and derivatives of the posterior mean (or, alternatively, of the ‘score’ function). This second-order information contained in pre-trained diffusion models can be distilled into parametric models of the covariance, either by differentiating through the score network exactly ( 29 ) or approximately ( 23 ) , or by reformulating the posterior covariance as the minimum mean squared error (MSE) estimator of a quantity involving the posterior mean ( 26 ; see also Background ). However, for models that generate color images with D = d 2 D=d^{2} pixels, the full posterior covariance matrix (or, equivalently, its square root) has a large memory footprint ( 3 ​ D × 3 ​ D 3D\times 3D ) implying 𝒪 ⁡ ( D 2 ) \mathcal{O}(D^{2}) sampling complexity, calling for more tractable approximations. This tradeoff is not unlike that encountered in neural network optimization, where accurately modeling the (second-order) curvature of the loss enables the use of larger learning rates, yet loss Hessians are large objects that can only be estimated in approximate, memory-efficient forms ( 24 ; 12 ; 13 ) . 31 have recently leveraged this connection to improve image restoration. All recent attempts at modeling denoising posterior covariances have assumed a diagonal or low-rank structure, which we argue is very restrictive. Here, we develop a new covariance model for image DDPMs ( Figure 1 A) which accurately and efficiently captures the strong yet non-diagonal spatio-chromatic correlations between both neighbouring pixels and color channels present in natural images ( Figure 1 B; 5 ; 7 ; 11 ). These chromatic and spatial correlations are approximately separable ( 30 ) , and therefore Kronecker-factorizable, and the spatial component can be compactly represented in the frequency domain of the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) owing to approximate translation invariance ( 17 ) . The resulting ‘K-DCT’ model is described in detail in Section 3.2 ; Figure 1 B (bottom) shows that it provides a good fit to the marginal (i.e. prior) CIFAR-10 covariance, and this paper explores its use for approximating the posterior covariances that arise in image denoising – an example of which is shown in Figure 1 C (top) along with its best K-DCT approximation (bottom). Starting from pre-trained score models, we learn K-DCT-structured amortizations of the (input-dependent) posterior covariance Cov ​ ( 𝒙 t − δ | 𝒙 t ) ≈ K-DCT ​ ( 𝒙 t , θ ) \text{Cov}(\bm{x}_{t-\delta}|\bm{x}_{t})\approx\text{K-DCT}(\bm{x}_{t};\theta) . On CIFAR-10, Celeb-A, ImageNet and LSUN, we show that in the regime of few sampling steps, this leads to both better image generation (lower FID; 14 ) and better statistical models (lower negative log-likelihood) compared to previous diagonal approximations. sections.heading: 2 Background
sections.text: In this section, we begin by providing important background on the general Gaussian denoising problem, highlighting two ways of obtaining the mean and covariance of the denoising posterior distribution. We then discuss how these two denoising strategies can be applied to the sampling process in DDPMs, which we also summarize.

sections.heading: 2.1 The Gaussian denoising problem
sections.text: Consider a random vector 𝒙 ∈ ℝ n \bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} drawn from some distribution q ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) q(\bm{x}) . Given a noisy observation 𝒙 ~ ∼ q ⁡ ( 𝒙 ~ | 𝒙 ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝒙 ~ , 𝒙 , σ 2 ​ I ) \tilde{\bm{x}}\sim q(\tilde{\bm{x}}|\bm{x})=\mathcal{N}(\tilde{\bm{x}};\bm{x},\sigma^{2}I) , what can be said about 𝒙 \bm{x} ? Whilst the posterior distribution q ⁡ ( 𝒙 | 𝒙 ~ ) q(\bm{x}|\tilde{\bm{x}}) is generally intractable (e.g. the prior q ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) q(\bm{x}) may not be Gaussian), there are at least two ways of obtaining its moments.

sections.heading: 2.2 Denoising diffusion probabilistic models
sections.text: DDPMs ( 15 ) are probabilistic models that allow sampling from an arbitrary distribution q ⁡ ( 𝒙 0 ) q(\bm{x}_{0}) . Just as in the Gaussian denoising problem discussed above, DDPMs define a whole collection of noisy observations { 𝒙 1 , … , 𝒙 T } \{\bm{x}_{1},\ldots,\bm{x}_{T}\} , obtained by sequentially down-scaling, and adding Gaussian noise to, each data sample 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} : 𝒙 t = α t ​ 𝒙 t − 1 + β t ​ ϵ t with ϵ t ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) , \bm{x}_{t}=\sqrt{\alpha_{t}}\bm{x}_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_{t}}\bm{\epsilon}_{t}\quad\text{with}\quad\bm{\epsilon}_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), where β t \beta_{t} is a time-dependent diffusion coefficient also known as the ‘noising schedule’. Typically, α t = 1 − β t \alpha_{t}=1-\beta_{t} , a choice that preserves the total variance of 𝒙 t \bm{x}_{t} at each step t t . Having introduced this forward ‘noising’ Markov chain, the data distribution can be expressed as q ⁡ ( 𝒙 0 ) = ∫ d ⁡ { 𝒙 1 , … , 𝒙 T } ​ q ​ ( 𝒙 T ) ​ ∏ t = 1 T q ⁡ ( 𝒙 t − 1 | 𝒙 t ) . q(\bm{x}_{0})=\int d\{\bm{x}_{1},\ldots,\bm{x}_{T}\}q(\bm{x}_{T})\prod_{t=1}^{T}q(\bm{x}_{t-1}|\bm{x}_{t}). Therefore, sampling from q ⁡ ( 𝒙 0 ) q(\bm{x}_{0}) can be achieved by sampling from q ⁡ ( 𝒙 T ) q(\bm{x}_{T}) and then running a sequence of small denoising steps whereby each 𝒙 t − 1 \bm{x}_{t-1} is obtained from 𝒙 t \bm{x}_{t} by sampling the relevant denoising posterior q ⁡ ( 𝒙 t − 1 | 𝒙 t ) q(\bm{x}_{t-1}|\bm{x}_{t}) . Critically, for a sufficiently long noising process, 𝒙 T \bm{x}_{T} is approximately normally distributed and is therefore trivial to sample. In general, each posterior q ⁡ ( 𝒙 t − 1 | 𝒙 t ) q(\bm{x}_{t-1}|\bm{x}_{t}) is intractable, and is normally approximated by a Gaussian: q ⁡ ( 𝒙 t − 1 | 𝒙 t ) ≈ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝒙 t − 1 , 𝝁 t − 1 ​ ( 𝒙 t ) , Σ t − 1 ​ ( 𝒙 t ) ) . q(\bm{x}_{t-1}|\bm{x}_{t})\approx\mathcal{N}\left(\bm{x}_{t-1};\bm{\mu}_{t-1}(\bm{x}_{t}),\Sigma_{t-1}(\bm{x}_{t})\right). (5) Note that it is possible to generate a sample 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} using a number of denoising steps smaller than T T , by merging any number of consecutive denoising steps into a single one (‘skip-step DDPM’). This is done by leveraging the fact that, under the noising model, any 𝒙 t \bm{x}_{t} is a linear-Gaussian transformation not only of 𝒙 t − 1 \bm{x}_{t-1} but of any previous 𝒙 s < t \bm{x}_{s<t} . This leads to simple affine relationships between { 𝝁 t − 1 ​ ( 𝒙 t ) , Σ t − 1 ​ ( 𝒙 t ) } \{\bm{\mu}_{t-1}(\bm{x}_{t}),\Sigma_{t-1}(\bm{x}_{t})\} and the more general { 𝝁 s ​ ( 𝒙 t ) , Σ s ​ ( 𝒙 t ) } \{\bm{\mu}_{s}(\bm{x}_{t}),\Sigma_{s}(\bm{x}_{t})\} ( Section A.1 ). It is precisely when skipping steps that the posterior covariance becomes less diagonally dominant, such that it becomes important to accurately model its structure – the focus of this paper. We now discuss how estimates of 𝝁 t − 1 ​ ( 𝒙 t ) \bm{\mu}_{t-1}(\bm{x}_{t}) and Σ t − 1 ​ ( 𝒙 t ) \Sigma_{t-1}(\bm{x}_{t}) can be obtained.

sections.heading: Posterior covariance
sections.text: The posterior covariance function, Σ t − 1 ​ ( 𝒙 t ) \Sigma_{t-1}(\bm{x}_{t}) , is often approximated by one of two time-dependent, but 𝒙 t \bm{x}_{t} -independent, heuristics: β t ​ I \beta_{t}I (‘large’), or β ~ t ​ I \tilde{\beta}_{t}I (‘small’) with β ~ t ≜ 1 − α ¯ t − 1 1 − α ¯ t ​ β t \tilde{\beta}_{t}\triangleq\frac{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\beta_{t} . These become equal, and exact, in the limit of many small (de-)noising steps, i.e. a limit where 𝒙 0 \bm{x}_{0} contains much less information about 𝒙 t − 1 \bm{x}_{t-1} than does 𝒙 t \bm{x}_{t} . For realistically small horizons T T , however, the posterior covariance may be far from being a scalar, or even a diagonal matrix (e.g. Figure 1 C). Several works have sought to learn better models of the posterior covariance in parametric form. Similarly to the posterior mean function, the posterior covariance function Σ t − 1 ​ ( 𝒙 t ) \Sigma_{t-1}(\bm{x}_{t}) is mathematically related to the covariance of the noise, Cov ​ [ ϵ t | 𝒙 t ] \text{Cov}[\bm{\epsilon}_{t}|\bm{x}_{t}] , as follows: Cov ​ [ 𝒙 0 | 𝒙 t ] = β ¯ t α ¯ t ​ Cov ​ [ ϵ t | 𝒙 t ] , Σ t − 1 ​ ( 𝒙 t ) = β ~ t ​ I + β t 2 ​ α ¯ t − 1 ( 1 − α ¯ t ) 2 ​ Cov ​ [ 𝒙 0 | 𝒙 t ] . \text{Cov}[\bm{x}_{0}|\bm{x}_{t}]=\frac{\bar{\beta}_{t}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\text{Cov}[\bm{\epsilon}_{t}|\bm{x}_{t}],\,\,\Sigma_{t-1}(\bm{x}_{t})=\tilde{\beta}_{t}I+\frac{\beta_{t}^{2}\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}{(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})^{2}}\text{Cov}[\bm{x}_{0}|\bm{x}_{t}]. (7) Hence, to perform the denoising sampling step of Equation 5 given a pretrained model that already approximates the posterior mean of the effective noise term, it is sufficient to learn a parametric model ℰ ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) \mathcal{E}_{\phi}(\bm{x}_{t},t) of Cov ​ ( ϵ t | 𝒙 t ) \text{Cov}(\bm{\epsilon}_{t}|\bm{x}_{t}) . This model needs to have a manageable memory footprint, and its matrix square root (required for sampling) must afford computationally tractable matrix-vector products. The K-DCT covariance model we propose here is equally applicable to the two ways of obtaining posterior covariances described in Section 2.1 : either via derivatives of the score function (Tweedie’s 2 nd {}^{\text{nd}} -order formula), or via direct least-squares estimation from data. In the following, we describe their specific application to the DDPM denoising posterior.

sections.heading: Score derivative-based approach
MMSE approach
sections.text: 26 leveraged the least-squares estimator interpretation of the denoising posterior moments ( Section 2.1 ) to learn amortizations of higher-order derivatives of any data (log) distribution. In turn, they showed that a good second-order score approximation leads to better denoising uncertainty quantification. More recently, 2 followed a similar approach to fit a parametric model of Cov ​ ( ϵ t | 𝒙 t ) \text{Cov}(\bm{\epsilon}_{t}|\bm{x}_{t}) in the form ℰ ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) = diag ​ ( 𝜺 ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) ) \mathcal{E}_{\phi}(\bm{x}_{t},t)=\text{diag}(\bm{\varepsilon}_{\phi}(\bm{x}_{t},t)) , using a MMSE objective. Given independent ( 𝒙 0 , ϵ t ) (\bm{x}_{0},\bm{\epsilon}_{t}) pairs and the associated 𝒙 t = α ¯ t ​ 𝒙 0 + β ¯ t ​ ϵ t \bm{x}_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\bm{x}_{0}+\sqrt{\bar{\beta}_{t}}\bm{\epsilon}_{t} , their ‘noise prediction residual’ (NPR) objective reads ℒ NPR ​ ( ϕ ) = 𝔼 𝒙 0 ∼ q ⁡ ( 𝒙 0 ) ; ϵ t ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) ​ ‖ 𝜺 ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) − ( ϵ t − ϵ θ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) ) 2 ‖ 2 2 . \mathcal{L}_{\text{NPR}}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}_{0}\sim q(\bm{x}_{0});\bm{\epsilon}_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)}\left\|\bm{\varepsilon}_{\phi}(\bm{x}_{t},t)-\left(\bm{\epsilon}_{t}-\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{t},t)\right)^{2}\right\|^{2}_{2}. (10) This objective again relies on a pretrained first-order noise predictor ϵ θ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) \bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{t},\!t) . Similar to the OCM objective, we will adapt the NPR objective to deal with more general, non-diagonal covariance models.

sections.heading: 3 Covariance Parameterizations
sections.text: Tractable evaluation and differentiation of both the OCM ( Equation 8 ) and NPR ( Equation 10 ) objectives places constraints on the form of covariance approximation ( ℰ ϕ ​ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{E}_{\phi}(\cdot) ) that may be used. One highly flexible, but also highly intractable, choice would be to parameterize the Cholesky factor of the entire 3 ​ D × 3 ​ D 3D\times 3D covariance matrix, where D = d 2 D=d^{2} is the number of image pixels – this leads to a prohibitive 𝒪 ⁡ ( D 2 ) \mathcal{O}(D^{2}) memory and compute complexity. In this work, we introduce a model ℰ ϕ \mathcal{E}_{\phi} that provides not only a better inductive bias for image generation than previous proposals (briefly reviewed below), whilst affording efficient training and sampling.

sections.heading: 3.1 Existing parameterizations
sections.text: As previously mentioned, a popular covariance approximation is the diagonal parameterization: e.g. 27 and 29 parameterize 𝜺 ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) ∈ ℝ 3 ​ D \bm{\varepsilon}_{\phi}(\bm{x}_{t},t)\in\mathbb{R}^{3D} such that ℰ ϕ diag ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) = diag ​ ( 𝜺 ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) ) ∈ ℝ 3 ​ D × 3 ​ D \mathcal{E}^{\text{diag}}_{\phi}(\bm{x}_{t},t)=\text{diag}(\bm{\varepsilon}_{\phi}(\bm{x}_{t},t))\in\mathbb{R}^{3D\times 3D} . This has 𝒪 ⁡ ( D ) \mathcal{O}(D) (linear) complexity in both training and sampling, but fails to take into account pairwise correlations between pixels. To capture the dominant patterns of pairwise correlations under the denoising posterior, 26 added a low-rank component to the diagonal, resulting in: ℰ ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) = diag ​ ( 𝜺 ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) ) + R ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) ​ R ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) ⊤ \mathcal{E}_{\phi}(\bm{x}_{t},t)=\text{diag}(\bm{\varepsilon}_{\phi}(\bm{x}_{t},t))+R_{\phi}(\bm{x}_{t},t)R_{\phi}(\bm{x}_{t},t)^{\top} (11) where R ϕ ∈ ℝ 3 ​ D × r R_{\phi}\in\mathbb{R}^{3D\times r} with r ≪ 3 ​ D r\ll 3D . However, we find that the eigenvalue spectra of image denoising posterior covariances tend to decay slowly (see also 41 ), such that r r might need to be fairly large to capture useful structure. This is corroborated by 26 ’s qualitative results on the MNIST dataset, where they used r = 50 r=50 (i.e. 6% of D D ) to obtain a posterior covariance approximation that contained the patterns of denoising uncertainty between digits that one would intuitively expect. In the CIFAR-10 example of Figure 1 C, capturing 90% of the variance in the denoising covariance matrix requires setting r = 635 ≈ 20 % ​ of ​ 3 ​ D r=635\approx 20\%\text{ of }3D . For larger images, such as those in the datasets we consider here (CelebA and ImageNet), better forms of approximation are needed that can capture the full rank of the posterior covariance without introducing an additional compute/memory tradeoff.

sections.heading: 3.2 Proposed K-DCT parameterization
sections.text: Motivated by key statistical properties of natural images (recall Introduction and Figure 1 ) and by the spectral theory of discrete cosine transforms, we propose the following covariance model for image DDPMs, with individual components explained in detail below: ℰ ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) = diag ​ ( 𝜺 ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) ) ⏟ diagonal baseline + C ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) ​ C ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) ⊤ ⏟ inter-channel ⊗ ( F ⊤ ⏞ horiz. ⊗ F ⊤ ⏞ vert. ) ​ diag ​ ( 𝝀 ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) ) ​ ( F ⊗ F ) ⏟ inter-pixel . \mathcal{E}_{\phi}(\bm{x}_{t},t)=\underbrace{\text{diag}(\bm{\varepsilon}_{\phi}(\bm{x}_{t},t))}_{\text{diagonal baseline}}+\underbrace{C_{\phi}(\bm{x}_{t},t)C_{\phi}(\bm{x}_{t},t)^{\top}}_{\text{inter-channel}}\otimes\underbrace{(\overbrace{F^{\top}}^{\text{horiz.}}\!\otimes\!\overbrace{F^{\top}}^{\text{vert.}})\text{diag}(\bm{\lambda}_{\phi}(\bm{x}_{t},t))\left(F\!\otimes\!F\right)}_{\text{inter-pixel}}. (12) • Diagonal baseline – This term absorbs any diagonal contribution that the second (Kronecker-DCT) term might not capture, thereby ensuring that the model is at least as expressive as previous diagonal models we compare to. • Outer Kronecker product – The second term models the approximately separable spatio-chromatic correlation structure of natural images, whereby e.g. the red and blue content of two pixels are correlated in the same way irrespective of where these two pixels are located ( 30 ) . Separability is achieved through a Kronecker product ( ⊗ \otimes ) of inter-channel (color) correlations and inter-pixel (spatial) correlations, with each component modeled as follows: – Inter-channel ( 3 × 3 3\times 3 ) – The correlation between RGB channels is captured in full by the C ϕ ​ C ϕ ⊤ ∈ ℝ 3 × 3 C_{\phi}^{\vphantom{\top}}C_{\phi}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3} term. – Inter-pixel ( d 2 × d 2 d^{2}\times d^{2} ) – For the spatial component, we reason that natural images – seen as continuous functions of the infinite plane – have an approximately translation invariant distribution. Thus, their covariance operator has the Fourier modes as eigenfunctions ( 17 ) . For discretized (finite-size) images, the first practical parameterization that comes to mind is a diagonal matrix in the orthonormal basis given by the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) matrix. However, the DFT assumes cyclic boundary conditions which natural bounded images do not have – in other words, their covariance is not circulant (as a DFT-based model would assume) but rather Toeplitz ( 31 ) . In fact, empirically we find that the CIFAR-10 marginal covariance, in both the horizontal and vertical image directions, is the superposition of a Toeplitz component and a Hankel (“90-deg rotated Toeplitz”) component ( Figure 1 B). This suggests using the discrete cosine transform (DCT) instead: matrices diagonalized by the DCT have indeed been shown theoretically to possess precisely this Toeplitz + Hankel structure ( 36 ) . * Eigenbasis – We therefore consider a spatial covariance diagonalized by the 2-dimensional DCT operator F ⊗ F F\otimes F , which applies the standard 1-dimensional DCT operator F ∈ ℝ d × d F\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} ( 39 ) to both the vertical and horizontal image dimensions (note that F − 1 = F ⊤ F^{-1}=F^{\top} ). * Eigenvalues – The D D eigenvalues are parameterized in positive real form as 𝝀 ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ) \bm{\lambda}_{\phi}(\bm{x}_{t},t) . Visual intuition for the expressiveness of this spatial covariance parameterization is given in Figure 4 . This model has a small, 𝒪 ⁡ ( D ) \mathcal{O}(D) memory footprint (i.e. the size of a single image). In the next two subsections, we show that it is also amenable to efficient, 𝒪 ⁡ ( D ​ log ⁡ d ) \mathcal{O}(D\log d) training and sampling.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments & Results
sections.text: In this section, we run experiments to validate our hypothesis that the K-DCT covariance model ( Equation 12 ) provides a better inductive bias for image DDPMs, leading to better generative models. We use previously published, first-order UNet models pre-trained on various datasets ( Table 4 ), add additional UNet heads to decode the various terms of our covariance model (details below), and optimize the parameters of these new heads w.r.t. the generalized NPR or OCM objectives. We systematically compare our approach with results previously reported for the same first-order models but with diagonal covariance approximations 1 1 1 Our code is built on previous work released by ( 29 ; 2 ) for fair comparison, and can be found in https://github.com/mtkresearch/highdiff . Our results are summarized in Figure 2 and Table 2 .

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.text: For evaluation, we focus on two key metrics: statistical goodness of fit as measured by the average negative log-likelihood (NLL; − log ⁡ p ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) -\log p(\bm{x}) ) of test images, and perceptual quality of generated images as measured by the FID ( 14 ) . We approximate the NLL via the standard evidence lower-bound ( 15 ) , − log q ( 𝒙 ) ≤ 𝔼 q log p ( 𝒙 0 : T : k ) q ( 𝒙 1 : T : k | 𝒙 0 ) ≡ − L ELBO ( 𝒙 ) -\log q(\bm{x})\leq\mathbb{E}_{q}\log\frac{p(\bm{x}_{0:T:k})}{q(\bm{x}_{1:T:k}|\bm{x}_{0})}\equiv-L_{\text{ELBO}}(\bm{x}) , where p ⁡ ( ⋅ ) p(\cdot) denotes the Markov denoising process, and k k denotes the number of skipped steps. The lower bound becomes tighter with more sampling steps, i.e. with smaller k k . Here we have conservatively evaluated all inverses and log determinants involved in the ELBO using direct Cholesky decompositions, but see Figure 9 for an efficient stochastic estimator that is applicable at scale ( Section A.7 ). As shown in the lower block of Table 2 , our K-DCT model consistently outperforms diagonal models in terms of NLL, regardless of the training objective used, be it score derivative-based (OCM) or MMSE-based (NPR). As expected, improvements are more significant in the case of fewer sampling steps where a diagonal covariance no longer provides a good approximation. These improvements in NLL are largely reflected in FID improvements (see upper block of Table 2 where FIDs were evaluated based on 50k generated samples), especially in more aggressive skip-step regimes (lower K K ) and for larger images. Although FID and NLL are known to be somewhat loosely related (e.g. the ‘squared-noise’ (SN) diagonal approximation tends to do well in terms of FID but poorly on likelihoods; 2 ), overall our K-DCT model exhibits the best tradeoff between these two evaluation metrics amongst all models ( Figure 2 ). Example samples generated by our method can be found in supplementary materials. To quantify the additional compute overhead that K-DCT introduces, we present FID against wall-clock sampling time in Figure 3 , where we also include experiments with the higher-resolution ( 256 × 256 256\times 256 ) LSUN Bedroom dataset. Lastly, we investigate the benefits of directly learning the eigenvalues in frequency-domain comparing to using a low-rank structure. The model performance in FID along with the computation complexity are shown in in Section A.8 , Table 8 . As expected, we find that our K-DCT model consistently outperforms “diag+low-rank” models, which in turn outperform purely diagonal models. With increasing rank (until r = 50 r=50 ( 4.8 % 4.8\% of max.) for CIFAR10 and r = 100 r=100 ( OPEN 2.4 % ) 2.4\%) for CelebA), the FID decreases but there is still a large gap between low-rank models and our full-rank K-DCT. To understand why, we examined the eigenvalue spectra of the posterior covariances at various points in the sampling process as shown in Section A.8 , Figure 10 . These eigenvalues exhibit a power-law decay spanning several ( > 3 ) (>3) orders of magnitude (especially mid-way through the denoising process), indicating that they cannot accurately be rank-truncated. Notice that the memory consumption of low-rank models increases significantly with higher ranks, while our model keeps negligible memory overhead. To investigate the harm of fixing to the DCT basis when the underlying data lacks translation invariance, (e.g. the CelebA dataset), we carried out some ablation studies by relaxing the spatial eigenbasis to learnable matrices (see details in Section A.9 ). The improvements are only modest – much smaller than the improvement made by the original K-DCT over a purely diagonal model ( Table 9 ).

sections.heading: 5 Discussion & Limitations
sections.text: In summary, modeling important elements of natural image statistics can be done in an efficient way through our K-DCT parameterization, and improves image DDPMs especially in the regime of few denoising steps. Given how strongly non-diagonal denoising posterior covariances are ( Figure 1 C, top), and how much of this non-diagonal structure the K-DCT model appears to capture ( Figure 1 C, bottom), it is perhaps surprising that the performance gains are not more striking; in particular, it is difficult to match FID results from distilled models (e.g. 45 ; on the other hand, these one-step models lack a tractable likelihood). Perhaps a fundamental limitation of the broader ‘covariance modeling approach’ is that denoising posteriors in the skip-step regime are far from Gaussian, such that Gaussian sampling is not appropriate even with the right covariance. This problem is analogous to that encountered in second-order optimization, whereby modeling the curvature of the loss function leads to larger, more aggressive parameter updates, but these can easily leave the ‘trust region’ where the underlying quadratic approximation is valid. In the same way that second-order optimization benefits strongly from adaptive damping ( 25 ) , second-order sampling might benefit from input-dependent adaptation of the step size (implicitly damping the posterior covariance). Finally, while the generalizability of our method to non-image data remains an open question, it could potentially be applied to other domains where data exhibits approximate translation invariance, such as audio and speech (see Figure 11 for a proof of principle on speech data). In fact, perhaps paradoxically, one of the datasets where our K-DCT model performed best (relative to diagonal models) is CelebA, i.e. images of faces that clearly lack translation invariance. Thus, we speculate that K-DCT-like ‘full’ covariance models that model non-diagonal elements even crudely may lead to performance gains even when the underlying data lacks symmetries.

sections.text: Figure 4 shows the basis functions from which the spatial (achromatic) component of Equation 12 is assembled parametrically. Left : normalized MSE (black) obtained when approximating the marginal ImageNet covariance Σ \Sigma by a sum of n n spatio-chromatic Kronecker products (“ colors ​ ( 3 × 3 ) ⊗ pixels ​ ( d 2 × d 2 ) \text{colors}(3\times 3)\otimes\text{pixels}(d^{2}\times d^{2}) ”). The optimal decomposition of order n n has an analytical form ( 42 ) . Our approximation in Equation 12 corresponds to n = 1 n=1 , and is nearly perfect here; this best single Kronecker product approximation is shown at the top, along with the two corresponding factors. We will call the spatial factor S ∈ ℝ d 2 × d 2 S\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}\times d^{2}} ). For comparison, we also show the SVD-based rank- n n truncation of Σ \Sigma (green). Right: normalized MSE (black) obtained when approximating the spatial factor S S (c.f. above) with a sum of vertical-horizontal Kronecker products ( [ d × d ] ⊗ [ d × d ] [d\times d]\otimes[d\times d] ). For n = 1 n=1 , this type of approximation is close to, but not exactly the same, as what we propose in Equation 12 for modeling the spatial component. It would be the same if (i) we constrained our D ≡ diag ​ ( 𝝀 ) D\equiv\text{diag}(\bm{\lambda}) to itself be a Kronecker product of two smaller diagonals, but (ii) learned the eigenbasis instead of forcing it to be the DCT matrix F F . Again, a single unconstrained Kronecker product provides an excellent approximation here, indicating that a Kronecker-structured eigenbasis is empirically justified. Moreover, fixing the eigenbasis to F F but still learning a full diagonal D D (our main proposal) does nearly as well (dashed red; ( F ⊗ F ) ⊤ ​ D ​ ( F ⊗ F ) (F\otimes F)^{\top}D(F\otimes F) ) whilst having lower computational complexity. Figure 6 : Same as Figure 5 , but for modelling the CelebA marginal (i.e. prior) covariance. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the spatio-chromatic structure of this particular dataset is not as separable as for ImageNet; this is likely due to certain locations in the image being dominated by certain colors (e.g. celebrities aren’t known for their blue noses). It is also less translation invariant (i.e. less diagonalizable in the DCT eigenbasis) owing to the nature of these centered portraits. Figure 7 : Accuracy of Equation 12 for modeling conditional covariances at different stages of denoising (time t t ) on CIFAR-10. Left : at each time, we have a “true” covariance obtained by differentiating through the score network (c.f. Section 2.1 ) shown in the first row of images. As in Figures 5 and 6 , for each of these matrices we can find its nearest “diagonal + spatio-chromatic Kronecker product” approximation (second row). This yields a fairly good reconstruction MSE (black), much better than the nearest “diagonal + rank-1” approximation (green; third row of images). Both approximations were obtained through optimization. Right : at each time, we can then focus on the spatial component of the Kronecker product identified on the left, and approximate it in the same ways as we did in Figure 5 (right) with n = 1 n=1 . This is shown with the same color code. In summary, we see that at all times, the use of Kronecker products at both levels outperforms low-rank forms, and that reducing the complexity by restricting the spatial component to a DCT-diagonalized form does not hurt much.
